title: The More AI Helps You Refinance, the More Expensive Your Mortgage Gets
dek: Cheap US mortgages partly rely on most borrowers being too lazy to refinance when rates drop. Once AI agents remind everyone to refinance in time, that option gets repriced and mortgage rates actually rise.
why: This episode pushes the consequences of 'AI removing friction' to the extreme: the money you think you save gets repriced away by the financial system. The second half covers phantom bidding in Amazon's ad auction and ETF dividend timing trades.
who: People in mortgages, asset management, law firm management, and ad auction operations, plus any founder concerned with how AI removing friction changes the pricing of financial products.
skip: The first about 4 minutes of pleasantries and self-introduction can be skipped; from minute 5, when it gets into AI refinancing, there is almost no filler.

points.h: AI reminders to refinance make mortgages more expensive
points.body: US homeowners generally do nothing when rates fall: Matt met someone on a plane who was telling him about his mortgage rate and was about to sell and buy a bigger house, and Matt talked him out of it on the spot. Morgan Stanley research argues that if an AI agent reminds you to refinance when rates drop by 200 basis points, future refinancing will be much easier. Sounds like saving you money, but more frequent refinancing means the prepayment option that people used to 'neglect to exercise' actually gets exercised, lenders reprice for that, and everyone's mortgage rate rises by 10 to 20 basis points.

points.h: The smarter homeowners are, the fewer people can buy homes
points.body: Fabrice Touré—former head of mortgage derivatives at Goldman Sachs, now a finance academic—puts it bluntly in his paper: policies that make refinancing more frequent also raise the equilibrium mortgage rate and reduce the likelihood that many borrowers get credit. The reason is that the US 30-year fixed-rate, prepayable mortgage carries an expensive option, but most people exercise it poorly, which is why lenders are willing to charge lower rates. Once institutions or AI make everyone more rational, the option gets repriced, rates rise, fewer people are covered by the low-rate subsidy, and more families cannot afford a home.

points.h: Models priced on past behavior will get blindsided
points.body: The shock hits investors first. Morgan Stanley warns that historical prepayment behavior will underestimate future prepayments: any model trained on past data misprices 'borrowers being more willing to exercise the prepayment option.' As a result, some mortgage-related assets look cheap but are actually built on the assumption that borrowers stay lazy; when AI cuts refinancing friction from two weeks to ten minutes, those assets all need to be revalued. Matt extends the logic: credit card points, high-yield savings accounts, life insurance policies—all the same. The financial system largely runs on customers not using every option to the fullest.

points.h: AI makes the billable hour model obsolete
points.body: The squeeze on professional services shows up first at law firms: clients think AI can do the work of a squad of junior associates and demand lower rates. Firms bill by the hour on the surface, but the real money comes from partners selling junior associates' hours at a high price and paying them a lower wage; if AI handles a lot of the grunt work, 'charging for junior associate hours' no longer holds. Senior lawyers' judgment is still valuable, but it needs a different pricing model. The bigger issue: when juniors no longer spend hundreds of hours on basic work, where do the future partners develop their instincts?

points.h: Top partners can fly solo with AI
points.body: Since a senior lawyer's value is not realized through headcount, the very best will do the math first: rather than stay in a big platform to support a partner committee and train a cadre of juniors, they will leave and open a boutique with just themselves and six AI agents. Chris Kircher, a former Quinn Emanuel partner, has already resigned to start an AI-native law firm built on that bet. If enough senior people leave, big firms cannot retain them even knowing the apprenticeship model matters—the profit-generating capacity leaves, the money-losing training system stays, and big firms struggle to survive.

points.h: Amazon's auction hides a phantom bidder
points.body: The FTC and attorneys general from 22 states sued Amazon, saying its ad auction is not the second-price auction it advertises. In a normal second-price auction, the highest bidder pays the second-highest bid; Amazon adds a 'soft reserve price'—the platform's own valuation of the ad slot, like a bidder hiding in the dark. If your bid is above the soft reserve, the soft reserve becomes the second price; if your bid is below, the winner pays their own maximum bid instead. Amazon's response: the ad auction is a real-time black box, no one can know the soft reserve in advance, and advertisers just look at return on ad spend.

points.h: Bidding against the chandelier is legal
points.body: The financial world forbids exchanges from secretly placing their own buy orders, but art auction houses have a legal performance. The seller sets a secret reserve price; when live bids are not enough, the auctioneer calls out bids into empty air, pushing the price up to the reserve—the term is 'chandelier bid,' because he often looks up at the chandelier. New York requires auction catalogs to disclose that the auctioneer may bid on behalf of the seller up to the reserve and will not indicate which bids come from the seller. Amazon's soft reserve is likewise the platform bidding for itself, but without such a fine-print disclosure—that is exactly what the FTC is seizing on.

Foreign funds (e.g., Cayman structures) pay withholding tax on US stock dividends, which drags on the thin margins of basis trades. In the market, some players use two nearly identical S&P 500 ETFs with a timing difference: BlackRock's IVV and Vanguard's VOO pay dividends about a week apart. The maneuver: sell IVV before its ex-dividend date and switch into VOO; then switch back when VOO is about to pay. After the ex-date, the fund price drops by roughly the dividend amount, so the investor avoids the taxed dividend and earns the same money back by selling high and buying low. This is an institutional tax play; retail investors copying it would generate large capital gains taxes—not a TikTok money tip.

terms.def: The highest bidder wins but pays only the second-highest bid.
A hidden floor price set by the platform or seller in an auction, effectively adding a phantom bidder.
An auctioneer bidding on behalf of the seller into empty air to push the price toward the reserve; named because he often looks up at the chandelier.
Simultaneously buying the spot asset and selling the futures contract to capture the spread; essentially providing funding.
The pattern in professional services where juniors do large amounts of low-level work and gradually develop into senior partners.
A tax deducted at source on payments such as dividends; foreign investors are often subject to it.
